analysis.one_liner: Guarantees post-conviction DNA testing, qualified lawyers in death penalty cases, and compensation for the wrongly convicted.
analysis.headline: The Innocence Protection Act, which would have guaranteed DNA testing for inmates claiming innocence, died in a House subcommittee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have given prisoners a way to get DNA testing on old evidence that could prove them innocent, required the government to preserve that evidence instead of destroying it, and pressured states to do the same by tying federal crime grants to those rules. It also would have set minimum standards for lawyers appointed to death penalty cases and raised compensation for people who were wrongly imprisoned. It was introduced in the House in March 2000 and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: People in prison who say DNA testing could prove them innocent, especially those sentenced to death, would gain a right to have the evidence tested at government expense if they are indigent [S2][S3]. Indigent capital defendants would gain access to qualified, adequately paid lawyers through a new grant system [S2]. People later proven wrongly convicted would gain compensation of up to $50,000 per year of imprisonment, or $100,000 per year for those who were sentenced to death [S2][S3]. The public also stands to gain: the bill's findings note cases where post-conviction DNA testing freed an innocent person and identified the actual perpetrator [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Gives any federal prisoner the right to ask a court for DNA testing of evidence in the government's possession, and requires the government to preserve biological evidence for as long as anyone remains imprisoned for the case
Bars states from denying DNA testing requests or using time limits and procedural default rules to block exculpatory DNA results, enforceable in a civil action with no immunity for state officers

Conditions federal DNA, Byrne, and policing grants on states preserving evidence and offering DNA testing on the same terms as the federal system, and requires certified quality-assurance and proficiency testing for laboratories receiving grant funds

Requires death penalty states to certify an effective system of competent legal services for indigent capital defendants as a condition of Byrne grants, and creates new capital representation grants with market-rate compensation for appointed attorneys

Raises compensation for people unjustly imprisoned in federal cases to up to $50,000 per year, or $100,000 per year for those sentenced to death, and requires annual public reports on how capital punishment is administered, including racial data on death-eligible defendants and juries

analysis.who_pays: Federal and state governments would bear the costs: paying for DNA testing for inmates who cannot afford it (courts could bill non-indigent applicants), preserving biological evidence for as long as anyone remains incarcerated, paying capital defense attorneys market rates with support staff, and compensating the wrongly convicted up to $50,000 per year imprisoned ($100,000 for those sentenced to death) [S2][S3]. States would also face new conditions on federal justice grants, including evidence preservation and DNA testing requirements, as the price of receiving the money [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The bill would cost taxpayers money: government-funded DNA testing, long-term evidence preservation, market-rate pay for capital defense attorneys, and compensation of $50,000 to $100,000 per year of wrongful imprisonment
The bill presses states to change their rules by attaching conditions to federal grant money, which states could view as federal overreach into their own criminal justice systems

Even for a person proven innocent, compensation remains capped, and the federal death penalty provision still allows the Attorney General to seek execution in states that forbid it by simply certifying one of several listed exceptions

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill aimed its protections at a small group — prisoners whose innocence DNA testing could establish, mostly those facing execution — but the stakes for that group are as high as they get: life or death. The costs to governments are real but modest by federal standards, and the bill itself notes the typical DNA test cost only $2,400 to $5,000 [S3]. Its main weaknesses are that it relies on grant conditions rather than outright mandates on states, keeps compensation capped, and leaves the Attorney General a wide exemption to pursue federal death sentences in anti-death-penalty states. On balance it would have shifted modest public money to prevent the imprisonment or execution of innocent people.

outcome.mechanism: The bill attracted no cosponsors, was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and then its Crime Subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the House on March 23, 2000, with Rep. Alcee Hastings as its sole sponsor and no cosponsors
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction, and to the Crime Subcommittee about two weeks later
No further action was taken; the bill was never debated, voted on, or passed by either chamber before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: State criminal justice systems and prosecutors kept full discretion over biological evidence and faced no new grant conditions. Incarcerated people claiming innocence, and the wrongly convicted, gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Prosecutors and states kept the status quo

for.name: Rep. Alcee L. Hastings
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: House Committee on the Judiciary / Subcommittee on Crime
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Crime Subcommittee, which took no further action on it before the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and no recorded opposition, so its partisan shape is unknown.

industries.industry: State criminal justice systems and prosecutors
industries.note: The bill would have required states to preserve biological evidence and give inmates access to DNA testing as a condition of federal justice grants, and stripped their ability to use time limits and procedural rules to block DNA results. Prosecutors would have lost a source of leverage and states would have lost discretion over grant funds.

Laboratories would have faced mandatory quality-assurance standards and twice-yearly proficiency testing before receiving federal DNA grant money, but the same certification requirements would have steered federal DNA funding through accredited labs.

industries.industry: Federal prosecutors and the Justice Department
industries.note: The Department of Justice would have had to pay for testing, preserve evidence, produce annual reports on the administration of capital punishment, and curtail federal death penalty prosecutions in states that outlaw execution absent a written certification by the Attorney General.
